title: Sound & Waves Lab
subject: Physics
summary: A sandbox with three benches: a ripple tank wired to an oscilloscope, an open field and an echoing room, and a ship's sonar with an ultrasound scanner. Predict, play with the controls, measure, and explain what you saw.

scenarios.setup: A ripple tank connected to an oscilloscope. Sliders for frequency and amplitude.

tasks.prompt: The wave generator is running at {f1} Hz. Raise the frequency to {f2} Hz and watch the tank and the oscilloscope. Predict what will happen to the wavelength in the ripple tank.
tasks.expectedOutcome: The wavelength decreases. The wave speed (v = f × λ) stays constant in the same medium, so a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength.
tasks.anomalyExplanation: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional when the wave speed is constant (v = fλ). Higher frequency does not make the wave faster: it makes the waves closer together.

tasks.prompt: The generator is set to an amplitude of {a1} mm. Raise it to {a2} mm. Predict what will happen to the loudness of the sound, if this were a sound wave.
tasks.expectedOutcome: Loudness increases. Amplitude determines the intensity (loudness) of a sound wave.

scenarios.setup: An open field and a small empty room. A clap button and a stopwatch tool.

tasks.prompt: Clap your hands in the open field, then in the small room, whose sound dies away over about {rt} s. Predict the difference in what you will hear.

predictionOptions.label: A single clap in the field, and a prolonged sound in the room

tasks.expectedOutcome: A single clap in the field, and a prolonged, overlapping sound (reverberation) in the room due to multiple rapid reflections.

tasks.prompt: You shout towards a distant cliff and hear an echo {t} s later. The speed of sound in air today is {v} m/s. Predict the distance to the cliff, then measure the delay yourself with the stopwatch.
tasks.expectedOutcome: The sound travels to the cliff and back, so the cliff is half the total distance away: distance = (speed × time) / 2.
tasks.explanation: Distance = (speed × time) / 2. With {v} m/s and {t} s the sound covers {tot} m there and back, so the cliff is {d} m away.

scenarios.setup: A ship's sonar console with a pulse button and a timer. A cross-section of the ocean. An ultrasound scanner.

tasks.prompt: Send a sonar pulse towards {target}. The echo returns after {t} s, and the speed of sound in seawater is {v} m/s. Predict the depth, then send the pulse, read the timer and calculate the depth from your own reading.
tasks.expectedOutcome: The pulse travels down and back, so the depth is half the distance covered: depth = (speed × time) / 2.
tasks.explanation: Depth = (speed × time) / 2 = ({v} × {t}) / 2 = {h} m. The pulse travels to the target and back, so only half the distance is the depth.

tasks.prompt: An ultrasound scanner sweeps over a cyst {s} mm across. Compare the scan made with ordinary audible sound and with ultrasound. Predict why audible sound cannot be used for this.

predictionOptions.label: Normal sound has too long a wavelength to resolve small details
Normal sound is not safe for humans

tasks.expectedOutcome: Normal sound has too long a wavelength to resolve small details. Ultrasound has a much shorter wavelength, so it reflects off small structures such as organs and tissue.
tasks.explanation: Resolution is limited by wavelength. Higher frequency (ultrasound) means a shorter wavelength, which resolves smaller details.

examples: Bats, dolphins and sonar all use echoes
Auditoriums use soft panels to control reverberation
Echo-ranging to measure the depth of wells
uses.why: An echo is a reflection heard as a separate sound, which needs at least about 17 m to the reflector. In a small room the reflections overlap, which we hear as reverberation.

examples: Ships measure the depth of the sea
Submarines and survey vessels map the sea floor
uses.why: Sonar sends a pulse and times its echo: distance = (speed × time) / 2, because the pulse goes there and back.

examples: Scans of the unborn baby and internal organs
uses.why: Ultrasound's short wavelength lets it reflect from small structures, giving a sharp image where audible sound would blur everything.
